summary.headline: An outstanding debt-free app business, but at Rs 176 the price is about twice fair value
summary.text: Digital Mobility Solutions Lanka PLC (PickMe, PKME.N0000) runs Sri Lanka's leading ride-hailing and delivery app. It is an outstanding business: no borrowings, Rs 4.0bn of cash and deposits, return on equity of 71% over the last twelve months, and profit up 49% in the six months to September 2026, with a record September quarter (EPS Rs 2.35). This full redo (requested as /redo PKME full) rebuilt the research record from the three CSE reports using printed figures only, and moved every method into the site's valuation code. Fair value is now about Rs 83 (was Rs 97). The two main reasons: the P/E method now uses the stable-growth justified P/E rather than a hand-worked two-stage P/E, because the growth premium is already counted in the DCF and the dividend model; and the DCF's starting cash is taken from recorded figures rather than lifted by hand. At Rs 176 (CSE close, 20 November 2026) the share trades at 22x trailing earnings. To be worth that price, PickMe would need about 33% growth a year for seven years, or a required return near 13.7% against the 18.8% used here. I'd buy at up to about Rs 71 and treat under Rs 62 as a strong buy. The business tests still pass 3 of 4: an operating loss in 2021/22 fails the five-year steady-profit test. So it stays 'good' and on the watch list. The beta (1.03, from web-search stand-ins) is the biggest uncertainty: at a 16% cost of equity the base DCF alone gives about Rs 135.

valuation.note: Fair value averages three methods, each weighted bear/base/bull 30/50/20: the whole-company DCF plus fixed deposits (Rs 105.23), the justified P/E (Rs 57.92) and the dividend model (Rs 86.60). That gives Rs 83.25, about 10x trailing EPS. All values come from scripts/valuation.py. The cost of equity (18.8%) comes from the beta; WACC is the same because there is no debt.

Twelve months to September 2026 (company figures: 49%, 54% and 69% for the last three years). Very high because equity is small and payables to drivers fund working capital.

On trailing EPS of Rs 8.00 (18.7x the September quarter × 4). At an 18.8% cost of equity, the stable-growth justified P/E is 6.3x in the base case. The two-stage value of growth is in the DCF and the dividend model.

CAPM with a country premium, beta 1.03 (provisional).

models.name: Whole-company DCF + fixed deposits (WACC, less net debt)
models.comment: Starting cash before interest, after maintenance capex, is Rs 1.91 / 2.73 / 3.18bn. Bear is after-tax operating profit plus depreciation; base is 2025/26 operating cash; bull is operating cash for the twelve months to September 2026. Each takes off maintenance capex of Rs 0.89 / 0.69 / 0.69bn. After-tax operating profit starts at Rs 2.11 / 2.50 / 2.88bn: 2025/26, the last twelve months, and the September quarter × 4, at the 30.9% tax rate. Both grow 12% / 18% / 24% a year for seven years, then 5% / 6% / 7%. Each year the DCF takes off the reinvestment that growth needs, at a 40% / 60% / 80% return on new capital, falling to 25% / 30% / 35% after year seven. Discounted at WACC 20.3% / 18.8% / 17.3%. Net cash of Rs 1.40bn is added back, plus the Rs 2.28bn of fixed deposits (Rs 6.83 a share). The value from after year seven is 48% / 57% / 66% of the total, under the 75% flag.

models.name: P/E method (stable justified P/E)
models.comment: EPS for the year to March 2027 is Rs 8.75 / 9.32 / 9.70: H1 Rs 4.24 plus a second half 20% / 35% / 45% above last year's Rs 3.76. The P/E is 5.2x / 6.3x / 7.8x, the stable-growth P/E justified at the cost of equity: (1 − growth ÷ ROE) ÷ (cost of equity − growth), with growth 5% / 6% / 7% and long-run ROE 25% / 30% / 35%. That growth is close to the 5.8% that reinvestment supports, so this is the value with no premium for the fast-growth years. Base EPS is 0.9% below the run-rate (September quarter × 4 = Rs 9.40); bear is 6.9% below, allowing for fuel or competition setbacks.

models.name: Dividend model (two-stage)
models.comment: Dividends start at the current 65% payout of the same EPS (Rs 5.7 / 6.1 / 6.3 this year). They grow 12% / 18% / 24% for seven years. After that, profit grows 5% / 6% / 7% with an 80% payout (1 − growth ÷ ROE). Discounted at 20.3% / 18.8% / 17.3%. Dividend growth is within profit kept × ROE (24%). Cash after maintenance capex covered 2025/26 dividends 3.2x, so the dividend isn't at risk.

modelsNote:
PickMe turns its profit into cash, so a whole-company DCF suits it, with a justified P/E and a dividend model alongside. NAV, P/B and residual income are left out because book value (Rs 13) is tiny next to earnings. All three methods are calculated by scripts/valuation.py from the inputs saved in the analysis.

**Growth check:** 12% / 18% / 24% a year is assumed for seven years. The growth supported by 2025/26 reinvestment is only 5.8%: reinvestment of 5.0% of after-tax operating profit × a 116% return on capital. All three cases are far above it. They are kept because the growth is already happening without capital: revenue rose 49% in 2025/26 and 38% in the first half of 2026/27, while reinvestment was only Rs 0.11bn. Most growth costs (incentives, marketing, most engineering pay) are charged against profit, drivers own the vehicles, and driver payables fund working capital. Profit kept × ROE gives 24%, above all three. The DCF also charges 20–30% of profit a year as reinvestment, far more than the business has needed. The P/E method uses only long-run growth of 5–7%, close to the supported rate.

**Ratio checks:** beta 1.03, cost of equity 18.8% and WACC (equal to it, with net cash) are within the normal ranges. ROE of 70% is far above the 15% test. It is right for this company: equity is small, it holds no plant, and payables to drivers fund working capital. Lease cost of debt is 13.7%, within range of the 12.24% bond yield.

assumptions.label: Cash before interest after maintenance capex, start

scenarios.common: The required return comes from CAPM with a country premium: risk-free 8.24% (the 12.24% 10-year bond less a 4.0% default spread), mature-market premium 4.2% plus country premium 6.08%, beta 1.03 (provisional). There are no borrowings, so WACC equals the cost of equity. The lease cost of debt (13.7%) has no weight because of the net cash. Tax is 30.9%, the 2025/26 effective rate. Maintenance capex is depreciation plus software amortisation (Rs 0.69bn), or in the bear case the two-year average capex booked (Rs 0.89bn). Long-run reinvestment = growth ÷ return on capital (5/25 = 20%, 6/30 = 20%, 7/35 = 20%). Per-share figures use 333.8mn shares. The fixed deposits (Rs 2.28bn) are added to the DCF at book.

fullText:
**Digital Mobility Solutions Lanka PLC (PickMe, PKME.N0000): full redo, 21 November 2026**

**Summary**
PickMe runs Sri Lanka's leading ride-hailing, delivery and trucking app. It is an outstanding business: it has no borrowings, Rs 4.0bn of cash and deposits, a 71% return on equity over the last twelve months, and profit up 49% in the first half of 2026/27. The September quarter was its best so far (EPS Rs 2.35). The share price already reflects much of this. At Rs 176 (CSE close, 20 November 2026) it trades at 22x trailing earnings and 13x book value. Fair value comes out at about Rs 83, using a required return of 18.8% from a provisional beta of 1.03.

- Fair value: **Rs 83.25** (was Rs 97.20)
- Buy price (15% below fair value): **Rs 70.76** (was Rs 82.60)
- Strong-buy price (25% below): **Rs 62.44** (was Rs 72.90)
- Business tests: 3 of 4, 'good'. Category 2, watch list (unchanged).

This redo (asked for as /redo PKME full) rebuilt the research record from the three CSE reports. It keeps only printed lines, stores each comparative column as its own period, and has the code work out the twelve-month figures, net debt and tax rate. All three methods now come from the site's valuation code. The code reproduces the old hand-worked DCF and dividend model exactly with the old inputs, so the fall in fair value comes from the inputs, not the formulas:
- The P/E method now uses the stable-growth justified P/E (5.2x / 6.3x / 7.8x) instead of a hand-worked two-stage P/E (6.5x / 9.4x / 14.7x). Reinvestment supports only 5.8% growth, and the fast-growth years are already valued in the DCF and the dividend model. This moves the P/E method from Rs 89 to Rs 58.
- The DCF's starting cash is now taken from recorded figures (Rs 1.91 / 2.73 / 3.18bn) instead of being set by hand at Rs 2.5 / 2.8 / 3.0bn.
- The return on new capital after the growth years now falls to 25% / 30% / 35%, as Damodaran recommends, instead of staying at 40% / 60% / 80% for ever. Together with the new starting cash, this moves the DCF from Rs 116 to Rs 105.
- The fixed deposits (Rs 2.28bn) are now valued as a separate add-on instead of being counted in net cash. The total is the same.

**Latest results**
- September 2026 quarter: revenue Rs 2.87bn (+37%), operating profit Rs 1.04bn (+48%), profit Rs 784mn (+53%). Monthly users about 2.1mn (+38%), driver earners +58%.
- Six months to September 2026: revenue Rs 5.38bn (+38%), operating profit Rs 1.88bn (+44%), profit Rs 1.41bn (+49%), EPS Rs 4.24 (Rs 2.85). Fuel rationing held back the June quarter.
- Twelve months to September 2026 (calculated): revenue Rs 10.17bn, profit Rs 2.67bn, EPS Rs 8.00, ROE 70.6% on average equity.
- Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 8.68bn (+49%), operating profit Rs 3.05bn (margin 35%), profit Rs 2.20bn (+88%), EPS Rs 6.61. Dividends Rs 4.30 (Rs 1.70 interim + Rs 2.60 final).
- Dividend: Rs 2.75 interim declared for 2026/27, at a 65% payout.

**Capex and reinvestment**
Capex booked in 2025/26 was Rs 0.96bn. Of that, Rs 0.81bn was the engineering pay capitalised as software, written off over four years; the rest was office fit-out and computers. Depreciation plus software amortisation was Rs 0.69bn. Right-of-use amortisation is left out, because leases are counted as debt. With no company split, maintenance capex is taken as Rs 0.69bn, or in the bear case the two-year average capex booked (Rs 0.89bn). The Rs 0.27bn above that is growth spending on the platform, so this was mostly a growth year, not a costly-to-run business. Working capital released Rs 0.16bn, because payables to drivers grow with volume. Net reinvestment was only Rs 0.11bn (5% of after-tax operating profit). There are no acquisitions and no named projects. R&D charged to profit isn't disclosed, and development is already capitalised, so no R&D adjustment is made. No warning signs: capex is paid from cash, not borrowing, and is above depreciation.

**Growth check**
Reinvestment supports only 5.8% growth (5.0% × a 116% return on capital). The scenarios assume 12% / 18% / 24% for seven years. They are kept for a specific reason: the growth is already happening without capital. Revenue rose 49% in 2025/26 and 38% in the first half of 2026/27, because incentives, marketing and most engineering pay are charged against profit, drivers own the cars, and payables fund working capital. Profit kept × ROE gives 24%, above all three cases. The DCF also charges reinvestment of growth ÷ 40% / 60% / 80% each year, far more than the business has needed.

**Valuation (Rs per share)**
| Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DCF + fixed deposits | 49.94 | 103.96 | 191.36 | 105.23 |
| Justified P/E | 45.75 | 58.25 | 75.34 | 57.92 |
| Dividend model | 53.04 | 85.13 | 140.60 | 86.60 |
| Average | 49.58 | 82.45 | 135.77 | **83.25** |

- **Required return:** risk-free 8.24% (12.24% bond less 4.0% default spread) + beta 1.03 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = 18.8% (bear 20.3%, bull 17.3%). With net cash, WACC equals the cost of equity.
- **DCF:** whole company, cash before interest after maintenance capex. Bear starts from after-tax operating profit plus depreciation (Rs 1.91bn), base from 2025/26 operating cash (Rs 2.73bn), bull from the last twelve months' operating cash (Rs 3.18bn). Growth is 12% / 18% / 24% for seven years, then 5% / 6% / 7%, less the reinvestment growth needs. The DCF then adds net cash of Rs 1.40bn and the deposits (Rs 6.83 a share). Value after year seven is 48% / 57% / 66% of the total.
- **P/E:** EPS to March 2027 of Rs 8.75 / 9.32 / 9.70 (base 0.9% below the Rs 9.40 run-rate) × the stable justified P/E.
- **Dividend model:** Rs 5.7 / 6.1 / 6.3 this year (65% payout), growing with profit for seven years, then an 80% payout.
- **Not used:** NAV, P/B and residual income, because book value (Rs 13.34) says little about an app business.

**Sensitivity:** even at a 17.3% WACC and 24% growth, the DCF gives about Rs 149. The price needs about 33% growth a year for seven years at 18.8%, or a WACC near 13.7% with base growth. Each 0.1 off the beta adds roughly Rs 10 to fair value.

**Buy plan for 500 shares**
- 200 shares at up to Rs 83.25
- 150 shares at up to Rs 70.76
- 150 shares at up to Rs 62.44
- Average about Rs 73.26, about Rs 36,630 in total (Rs 88,000 at today's price)

This isn't realistic soon. It needs a fall of more than half: the share has traded at Rs 134.75–175.25 since April 2026, and last traded near these levels in April–June 2025.

**Management and plans**
Management wants to expand every vertical across the island within two years, grow events, courier and bike-hailing, and push EVs and digital payments. It plans to use AI throughout and to keep minimal debt while paying out about 65% of profit. Technology spending is over Rs 1.6bn a year. Six months in, that is on track: revenue is up 38%, operating margin is improving, and the 65% payout has been kept.

**Shareholders**
Founder and CEO Zulfer Hassen holds 35.8% and Chairman Ajit Gunewardene 9.4%. In the September quarter, frontier funds and Capital Alliance added shares; director Ruchi Gunewardene sold 350,000. The public holds 50.2% across 6,548 holders.

**Risks**
- Price competition: the take rate was 10.3% in 2025/26.
- Fuel shortages.
- Regulation of ride-hailing and digital taxes.
- Tax disputes: income tax and VAT assessments under appeal, with contingent liabilities of Rs 0.84bn and Rs 1.66bn at March 2026, about Rs 7.50 a share together.
- Capitalised software running ahead of revenue.
- The beta, which rests on web-search stand-ins and is the biggest uncertainty in the valuation.

**What would change the view**
- Higher: a lower beta, faster growth for longer, lower rates, or a higher payout.
- Lower: a price war, fuel problems, losing the tax appeals, new rules, or a sharp slowdown.

management.takeaway: Management's plan is to keep the platform growing across Sri Lanka without debt, paying out about 65% of profit. Six months into 2026/27 that is on track: profit is up 49% with a 65% payout, though Rs 2.5bn of disputed tax and VAT is the risk to watch.

Keep strong liquidity and minimal debt while paying dividends
